title: Putin Says PM Modi Has 'Very Good Ideas' for Ending Ukraine Conflict
excerpt: The Russian president, speaking at the Valdai International Discussion Club, said Modi raises the issue of ending the war at every meeting and that Moscow is thankful for India's push for a peaceful settlement.
body:
• Russian President Vladimir Putin said PM Narendra Modi has "very good ideas" for a mutually acceptable settlement of the Ukraine conflict.
  • Putin made the remarks on October 1 at the annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club, as reported by state-run TASS.
  • The Russian leader said Modi raises the issue at "every meeting" and that Moscow is thankful for his desire to end the conflict through peaceful means.
  • The remarks come weeks after Putin and Modi held talks on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has publicly praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's efforts to end the Ukraine war, saying the Indian leader has "very good ideas" for finding a mutually acceptable settlement to the conflict.

Putin made the remarks on Thursday at the annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club, according to state-run news agency TASS. "As for Prime Minister Modi's position on ending wars, I can say that he is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good, even friendly relations, including at the personal level, constantly raises the issue and asks questions about ending the conflict in Ukraine," he said.

The Russian leader added that Modi "brings up these matters at every meeting we have and takes a keen interest in them." "He has very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions," Putin said.

"We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible."

— Vladimir Putin, President of Russia

Context & Background

Putin's comments build on a pattern of sustained India–Russia engagement. Ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September, Putin and Modi held talks during which the Russian leader briefed Modi on the situation in Ukraine, which began in February 2022, and on ongoing peace initiatives. Days before that, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia would welcome any peace efforts by India to end the conflict, noting that Moscow's strategy aligns closely with New Delhi's position of resolving the war through dialogue and diplomacy.

Modi has repeatedly stated India's position in similar terms. During a visit to Japan in August, he told The Yomiuri Shimbun that "India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy," adding that he encouraged "dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict." India has maintained diplomatic engagement with both Moscow and Kyiv throughout the war, alongside contact with Western capitals.

At the Valdai forum, Putin also expressed admiration for India's scale and diversity. "India cannot fail to amaze with its scale and diversity," he said, adding that Modi had told him 600 million of India's 1.5 billion people speak Hindi as their native language while the rest speak their own languages — "and they all live together — amazing."

Impact & Analysis

The remarks amount to public recognition from Moscow that New Delhi has a substantive voice in any conversation about ending the war — but they stop well short of evidence of a negotiated mediation process. No details of Modi's ideas have been made public, and coverage of the remarks stresses that they represent Putin's praise rather than acceptance of a specific proposal by Ukraine or Western partners.

That distinction matters. India has walked a careful line since February 2022: buying discounted Russian oil, abstaining on critical UN votes, sending humanitarian aid to Ukraine, and insisting publicly that "this is not an era of war." Putin's praise fits the narrative both capitals have cultivated — India as a credible interlocutor precisely because it talks to both sides. Whether Kyiv or Western partners engage with any Indian proposals remains the open question, and diplomats will be watching for statements from those capitals in response.

Diaspora Angle

The Indian diaspora — particularly in the United States and Europe — has watched India's balancing act with close attention, since the war has directly affected diaspora communities, from the evacuation of Indian students from Ukraine in 2022 to the economic ripple effects of energy prices and sanctions. Putin's comments will likely be read by diaspora audiences as validation of India's diplomatic weight, even as debate continues over whether New Delhi should do more.

What's Next

The immediate test is whether the rhetoric moves toward any formal process. No specific peace plan has been announced, and Ukraine's position on India's role is not publicly settled. With the war now in its fifth year, watch for whether the BRICS channel or other multilateral forums produce anything more concrete — and for responses from Kyiv and Western capitals to Putin's public endorsement of Modi's ideas.
